strengths: Proposes a well-motivated coordinate-free GUI grounding framework that aligns intrinsic MLLM attention with patch-wise supervision, avoiding extra grounding modules and a warm-up training stage.
Introduces a learnable <ANCHOR> token and a visual-sink query token based head-weighting mechanism, with clear formulation and supporting analysis in the appendix.
Achieves strong empirical results: state-of-the-art among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro and OSWorld-G and competitive performance on ScreenSpot-v2, using only ~85k training images.

Comprehensive ablations validate key design choices, including coordinate-free vs. embedding-based grounding, anchor token usage, visual-sink token selection, weighted patch labeling, and training efficiency.
The plug-and-play two-step zoom-in inference is simple, requires no additional training, and yields substantial gains on high-resolution screenshots.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and includes useful visualizations and convergence analysis.
weaknesses: The abstract's headline numbers (58.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.2% on OSWorld-G) require the optional two-step zoom-in; the base model achieves 45.2%/47.1% and 56.9%/56.5%, respectively. The claims should be more carefully qualified, and comparisons to single-step baselines may overstate practical gains.

Since all parameters are fine-tuned under attention supervision, the paper does not evaluate whether general MLLM capabilities such as captioning, VQA, or instruction following are preserved; this is important for a general-purpose GUI-agent backbone.

Novelty over prior attention-based coordinate-free methods such as TAG and GUI-Actor is incremental: the main additions are an <ANCHOR> token and heuristic head weighting via visual-sink query tokens.

The visual-sink query token selection and head-weighting strategy rely on several hyperparameters (top-k, global vs. layer-wise, soft matching) and are only validated on Qwen2.5-VL-3B; generalization across MLLM backbones is unverified.
The two-step zoom-in incurs extra inference cost, and its analysis is limited to ScreenSpot-Pro; the reported recovered/lost statistics would benefit from a more detailed protocol and error analysis.
Some implementation details are missing, such as patch size, visual token count, and data filtering/sampling specifics, and no code or limitations/societal-impact discussion is included.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem in GUI grounding with a well-motivated attention-based, coordinate-free framework that avoids generating explicit coordinate tokens and avoids adding task-specific grounding modules or an extra warm-up stage.

The proposed components are technically reasonable and mutually supportive: a learnable <ANCHOR> token to aggregate query-visual attention, attention-head weighting via visual-sink query tokens selected from hidden-state query-visual similarity, and overlap/distance-aware patch-wise labeling. The ablations in Table 4 support each design choice.

Empirical results are strong: GUI-AIMA-3B achieves state-of-the-art performance among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro (58.6% average with zoom-in) and OSWorld-G (62.2% average), while remaining competitive on ScreenSpot-v2, despite training on only ~85k screenshots / 259k instructions.

The two-step zoom-in inference is a practical, training-free enhancement for high-resolution screenshots, and the analysis in Table 5 and Section 4.3 provides useful insight into recovering offset errors.

The paper is generally clear, with good related-work positioning, informative figures, and transparent implementation details (backbone, batch size, learning rate, data sources), which aids reproducibility.

The data-efficiency claim is well supported: the method outperforms or rivals models trained on much larger datasets, which is a meaningful contribution for GUI grounding where large-scale data collection is costly.
The ablation study is thorough, comparing coordinate-free modeling manners, different Q_s selection strategies (global/layer-wise, top-k), soft weighting, and patch-labeling variants.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental relative to prior work such as TAG and GUI-Actor. The core idea of supervising MLLM attention for patch-wise grounding is already present in TAG, and GUI-Actor also explores coordinate-free grounding; the new ingredients here are the <ANCHOR> token and head-weighting strategy, which are useful but not a fundamental paradigm shift.

The 'coordinate-free' claim is slightly muddled by the statement that the method 'retain[s] the next-token prediction loss for GUI-AIMA's grounding format.' It is unclear exactly what the model outputs at inference and how the final click point is derived from the patch-wise attention prediction. The main text should specify this more precisely.

Visual-sink query token selection uses a top-1 global token chosen via hidden-state similarity. This appears potentially fragile, and the paper does not analyze failure cases or robustness across query types. The fact that the soft variant sometimes outperforms the hard variant on ScreenSpot-Pro suggests the chosen configuration may not be universally optimal.

General multimodal capabilities after fine-tuning are not evaluated. Because the method directly supervises attention maps, it is important to verify that it does not degrade general VLM abilities; the paper claims this is avoided but provides no direct evidence.

The paper does not include an explicit limitations or societal-impact discussion. Given that GUI agents can automate sensitive digital interactions, a discussion of risks, failure modes, and deployment considerations would strengthen the submission.

Some experimental details are sparse: the exact inference procedure from attention map to click point, the role of Q_s at inference time, and the selection of crop size/zoom factor are not fully specified in the main text.

The project page URL appears missing or truncated in the abstract, and no code release is mentioned. While implementation details are provided, reproducibility would be stronger with an available codebase or model checkpoint.

strengths: The core idea of exploiting intrinsic multi-head self-attention for coordinate-free GUI grounding, combined with an <ANCHOR> surrogate token, is reasonable and extends the attention-grounding line of work (TAG, GUI-Actor) in a coherent direction.

The empirical results are competitive at the 3B scale: 58.6% on ScreenSpot-Pro and 62.2% on OSWorld-G, with data-efficient training on ~85k screenshots, and the two-step zoom-in inference is a practical, training-free plug-in that demonstrably reduces offset errors (Table 5).

The ablation study in Table 4 is fairly thorough, isolating the effects of the anchor token, head weighting variants (uniform, all-query, <ANCHOR>, visual-sink), top-k selection, and patch-wise labeling, and providing convergence analysis (Fig. 4).
The writing is generally clear and the method is presented with reasonable formalization of attention aggregation and loss design.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. The framework is essentially a repackaging of TAG's attention-grounding with GUI-Actor's special-token idea; the <ANCHOR> token plays the same role as GUI-Actor's <ACTOR> token, and the claimed gains (e.g., ~4.5% over vanilla attention grounding) are modest. The paper does not clearly articulate what is fundamentally new beyond the previously published components.

There are evaluation gaps. The most directly comparable baseline, GUI-Actor-3B, is conspicuously absent from the main ScreenSpot-Pro table (Table 1 shows only GUI-Actor-7B, with '--' for GUI-Actor-3B), even though GUI-Actor-3B is the closest competitor. On ScreenSpot-v2 (Table 2), GUI-AIMA-3B (90.8) is not actually better than UI-TARS-7B (91.6) or JEDI-7B (91.7), so the claim of 'state-of-the-art among 3B models' is narrower than the presentation suggests.

Several design choices are heuristic and under-justified. The visual-sink query token selection relies on hidden-state cosine similarity with only top-1 chosen for the final model, and the justification for preferring hidden states over attention statistics is largely qualitative (Appendix A). The soft-matching variant Eq. (11) offers no clear advantage, and the paper does not establish why these particular heuristics should generalize across backbones or platforms.

The motivation for the <ANCHOR> token—that it 'learns to implicitly aggregate all query tokens'—is asserted rather than demonstrated; there is no probing/attention-visualization evidence that the anchor actually performs the claimed aggregation, and no analysis of when it fails (e.g., ambiguous or multi-region instructions).

The paper overstates its claims relative to the evidence: 'outperforms all models of similar sizes and rivals much larger MLLM-based GUI grounding models' is only partially supported, since several 7B baselines still lead on ScreenSpot-v2 and OSWorld-G in certain categories.

Reproducibility and responsible-research practices are underdeveloped: there is no limitations section, no societal-impact discussion, no statement on data licensing/attribution for the mixed training sources, and no indication of released code or model weights.

The two-step zoom-in results in Table 5 are reported only as a single benchmark analysis and the reported absolute numbers (e.g., 47.06 → 58.19) mix different error populations, making it difficult to compare fairly with one-step methods.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem in GUI grounding, proposing a coordinate-free attention-supervised framework that avoids text-based coordinate generation and extra grounding modules.

The <ANCHOR> token and visual-sink query token head-weighting are technically sound, well motivated, and validated by ablations; they improve over vanilla attention grounding and GUI-Actor under comparable training budgets.

The empirical results are strong at the 3B scale across five benchmarks, with notable data efficiency (509k samples/~101k screenshots) and a plug-and-play two-step zoom-in that substantially improves high-resolution GUI grounding.

The paper provides comprehensive analyses: ablations on aggregation and labeling, training convergence, attention-head pruning, two-step inference statistics, and qualitative examples in the appendix.
The writing is clear, the method is easy to follow, and the problem setting, metrics, and baselines are mostly well described.
weaknesses: The claim of 'state-of-the-art among 3B models' is overstated: Table 3 shows GroundNext-3B (RL) achieving 62.1% on UI-Vision versus GUI-AIMA-3B's 60.0%, and Table 2 shows GUI-Actor-3B + Verifier at 92.4% versus 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2. The claim should be qualified.

There is no direct comparison to TAG, the closest coordinate-free attention-based GUI grounding method; the vanilla attention ablation is not a full substitute for TAG, so the advantage over the most related prior work is not fully established.

The visual-sink query token selection is heuristic and relies on hidden-state similarity; it is not clear how robust this top-1 selection is across backbones, domains, or failure cases, especially since the selected tokens are often semantically uninformative sink-like tokens.

Some key design choices (single <ANCHOR>, top-1 token, global uniform selection, Gaussian labeling hyperparameters) are justified mainly empirically on a 45k ablation set, with limited theoretical grounding.

Reproducibility is somewhat limited: the project page is blank in the abstract, code is not provided, and many baseline numbers are taken from original papers rather than re-evaluated under a controlled protocol.

The two-step zoom-in requires an additional inference pass and crop, but the paper does not thoroughly report its computational overhead in the main experiments, and its sensitivity to crop size/zoom factor is only partially analyzed.

strengths: Well-motivated and cleanly formulated contribution: GUI-AIMA reframes GUI grounding as direct supervision over the MLLM's intrinsic multi-head self-attention with patch-wise signals, providing a natural alternative to indirect text-based coordinate generation.

The two key design elements are sensible and well justified: (i) an <ANCHOR> token placed after the GUI inputs to implicitly aggregate query-visual interactions and avoid impractical token-wise aggregation, and (ii) a head-weighting scheme derived from 'visual-sink query tokens' selected by hidden-state similarity, which is shown via Fig. 4 and Fig. 6 to concentrate on grounding-relevant heads (mid-to-late layers).

Strong data efficiency: GUI-AIMA-3B is trained with only 509k instructions (~101k screenshots), yet achieves state-of-the-art among 3B models on ScreenSpot-Pro (61.5% with zoom, 53.8% without) and ScreenSpot-v2 (92.1%), even beating substantially larger MLLMs on some benchmarks (e.g., GPT-4o and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B on ScreenSpot-v2).
Comprehensive evaluation across five benchmarks (ScreenSpot-Pro, ScreenSpot-v2, OSWorld-G, UI-Vision, MMBench-GUI-L2) spanning desktop, mobile, and web domains, with detailed per-category results.

Useful plug-and-play inference-time enhancement: the patch-wise grounding formulation naturally enables a two-step zoom-in procedure without additional training, with a quantitative analysis (Table 6) showing how offset errors are corrected and what is lost.

Ablations (Table 5, Table 10) isolate the contributions of anchored aggregation, visual-sink query token selection, and overlap/distance-aware patch labeling, and support the design choices quantitatively; convergence curves (Fig. 5) further show faster and more stable training than vanilla attention and GUI-Actor.
Clear, well-organized writing; the method figures (Fig. 2, Fig. 3) and head-weight visualization (Fig. 6) make the pipeline easy to follow.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental relative to closely related prior work. The paper builds directly on TAG's observation that MLLM attention maps already carry grounding signals, and the <ANCHOR> token is conceptually close to GUI-Actor's <ACTOR> token (embedding vs. attention). The claimed advance over TAG/GUI-Actor relies mainly on the specific aggregation and head-weighting choices, which are largely heuristic.

The visual-sink query token selection (Eq. 4–5) is an ad-hoc heuristic: cosine similarity between hidden states and visual patch states, aggregated across layers, with the top-1 token shared across layers. The justification ('sink-like behavior') is empirical and the 'visual-sink' terminology is applied post hoc; a more principled derivation would strengthen the contribution.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone (Qwen2.5-VL-3B). It is unclear whether the intrinsic-attention supervision and head-weighting mechanism generalize to other MLLM families or scales; without this, the generality claim is not fully supported.

The paper does not state whether code, model weights, or training data will be released, and key training details (e.g., the exact ground-truth format, the patch-grid resolution handling in Qwen2.5-VL) are only partially specified in the main text, which limits reproducibility.

There are minor internal inconsistencies in data description: Section 4.1 attributes the extra 250k desktop samples to 'GroundCUA (Feizi et al., 2025)', while Table 1's caption attributes them to 'GroundNext (Feizi et al., 2025) (710k)'. It is not clear whether these are the same dataset or different ones, and this affects the interpretation of the 'data efficiency' claim.

The two-step zoom-in procedure is a relatively standard test-time technique; its main novelty here is that it is 'free' due to the patch-level output, but the paper does not compare against existing zoom-in / crop-based approaches in the baselines.

The 'state-of-the-art among 3B models' claim is based on a subset of baselines that were trained with different data budgets and recipes (e.g., GUI-Actor-3B vs GUI-Actor-7B with verifier, GroundNext-3B RL with 710k), so the controlled comparison is only partial.

strengths: Strong and broad empirical evidence at the 3B scale: GUI-AIMA-3B reaches 53.8% (61.5% with zoom-in) on ScreenSpot-Pro, 92.1% on ScreenSpot-v2, 62.8% (68.1%) on OSWorld-G, 79.1% on MMBench-GUI-L2 and 60.0% on UI-Vision, matching or beating much larger models (e.g., UI-TARS-1.5-7B, JEDI-7B, GroundNext-7B) on several of these benchmarks. The core (non-zoom) ScreenSpot-Pro number is a genuine result at this parameter count.

Clear efficiency story: Table 8 shows 192 vs. 260 A100 GPU-hours relative to GUI-Actor-3B on the same 85k training set, the training set is 509k instructions / ~101k screenshots versus 9.6M samples for GUI-Actor, and the FlashAttention + selective-eager attention extraction limits the attention-map overhead to ~4.2% (Sec. 3.3).

The anchored-attention formulation (Eq. 2) is a clean and sensible simplification: it removes the impractical token-wise weighting of Eq. 1 while explicitly decoupling grounding supervision from the pre-trained query-token attentions, which is a defensible motivation for the <ANCHOR> design.

Ablations are reasonably systematic (Table 5 and Appendix Table 10): vanilla vs. simplified aggregation, uniform vs. <ANCHOR> vs. all-query weighting, layer-wise vs. global top-K token selection, and patch-wise labeling variants. Additional analyses (head pruning at 30%, Table 6 zoom-in offset statistics, Fig. 5 convergence) support the design choices.
The two-step zoom-in inference is genuinely plug-and-play, requires no additional training, and is quantitatively analyzed (Table 6) rather than merely asserted.
The paper is generally well organized and readable, with a clear statement of contributions and a coherent related-work positioning relative to coordinate-based and coordinate-free grounding.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty in an extremely crowded area. The attention-based grounding idea originates from TAG; the <ANCHOR> token closely parallels GUI-Actor's <ACTOR> token; and the patch-wise overlap/distance-aware label (Eq. 6) explicitly follows GUI-G². The remaining delta is (i) using the anchor's attention as the aggregated grounding vector instead of aggregating over all query tokens, and (ii) a heuristic head re-weighting. The component gains are small: +4.24% (ScreenSpot-Pro) from simplified aggregation, +1.9% from head weighting, +1.26% from patch labeling, all measured on the 45k ablation set where benchmark noise is comparable to these deltas.

No direct empirical comparison with TAG, the closest attention-based coordinate-free prior work. The 'vanilla attention grounding' baseline in Table 5 is the authors' own reformulation with uniform head weights, not TAG's published heuristic, so the claim that the proposed aggregation is superior to the prior attention-based aggregation is not actually established.

The head-weighting mechanism is under-justified and fragile. Selecting only the top-1 query token via hidden-state cosine similarity, aggregated globally across all layers, is a heuristic; Table 5 shows global top-1 vs. layer-wise top-1 differ by less than one point (42.13 vs. 41.43) and global top-3 is worse than top-1, which suggests the reported advantage is within benchmark noise. The claim that these tokens are 'functional proxies' for cross-modal interaction (Fig. 4) is asserted rather than demonstrated causally, and the design admits the more natural <ANCHOR>-based weighting works about as well (40.73).

The headline numbers are obtained with a test-time procedure that is not applied to baselines. The 61.5% ScreenSpot-Pro and 68.1% OSWorld-G figures in the abstract use the two-step zoom-in, while no baseline receives an analogous crop-and-rerun treatment, even though the procedure (predict coarse region, crop, re-predict) is largely method-agnostic. The abstract also mixes zoom-in and non-zoom-in numbers without labeling which is which, which overstates the 'state-of-the-art among 3B models' claim.

The 'coordinate-free' framing is partly semantic: the final prediction is still the argmax of a patch distribution over a grid, i.e., a coordinate estimate under a different parameterization. This is fine as a contrast to text-token coordinate generation, but the framing is stronger than the technical reality.

Evaluation is restricted to a single backbone family and scale (Qwen2.5-VL-3B); there is no evidence that the approach scales to 7B/30B backbones or transfers across architectures, which weakens the generality claim given that the method is presented as a general attention-supervision framework.

Some technical description is imprecise or inconsistent. 'The patch grid resolution is 28x28 in Qwen2.5-VL base model' conflates the 28x28 pixel patch size with a fixed patch grid; Qwen2.5-VL uses dynamic resolution with a variable number of visual tokens, so the fixed |V| and fixed patch geometry assumed in the labeling (Eq. 6) and in the two-step crop/zoom need clarification. The Gaussian parameter alpha = 0.8 is adopted from GUI-G² without sensitivity analysis, even though it directly controls the supervision target.

The data-efficiency narrative is diluted by the training mixture: GTA1 and UGround subsets are themselves derived/distilled data, and the final 250k GroundCUA instructions dominate the second stage. Without a controlled comparison separating data curation from the proposed supervision, the '509k samples is enough' claim is difficult to attribute to the method.
